title: Fundamental Solutions Newtonian Potentials and Green Functions

items.title: Fundamental solution of a constant-coefficient operator
items.statement: For a constant-coefficient differential operator $L=p(D)$ on $\mathbb R^n$, a distribution $E\in\mathcal D\prime(\mathbb R^n)$ is a fundamental solution when $LE=\delta_0$. Its translate $E_y(x)=E(x-y)$ satisfies $LE_y=\delta_y$, with translation defined on test functions and no conjugation in the pairing.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.title: Fundamental solution for the positive operator minus Laplacian
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: §2.6 equation (2.12) and one-dimensional analogue (2.13), printed p.33

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.title: Local integrability of the Laplace fundamental kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and n≥2. The normalized Laplace kernel Φ is locally integrable on R^n: its singularity is log|x| for n=2 and |x|^(2−n) for n≥3. It therefore defines a regular distribution.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.strategy: Use the chart/polar identification to know the sphere area is positive and finite, then apply polar integration to |Φ| on every centered ball. For n≥3 the normalized area cancels and the radial integrand reduces to r, integrating to R²/(2(n−2)); for n=2 the finite factor |S¹|/(2π) multiplies the integral of r|log r|, which is finite on (0,R) after splitting at R=1 when needed. Every compact set is measurable, bounded and lies in such a ball, so monotonicity gives local integrability. The regular-functional definition gives the pairing, and the Countable Choice local-L1 embedding theorem makes it a distribution.

items.title: The Laplace fundamental solution is harmonic off its pole
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. The displayed $\Phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ and satisfies $\Delta\Phi=0$ there; for every pole $y$, $x\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ is harmonic on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{y\}$.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.strategy: For a radial $q(r)$ compute $\Delta q=q\prime\prime+(n-1)q\prime/r$ directly from the Cartesian chain rule. Substitute $r^{2-n}$ for $n\ge3$ and $\log r$ for $n=2$, keeping the translation to $y$ explicit. The formula also gives $\partial_r\Phi=-1/(\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1})$ in either dimension.

items.title: The negative Laplacian of the fundamental solution is the unit Dirac distribution
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. The locally integrable kernel $\Phi$ defines a regular distribution and satisfies $-\Delta\Phi=\delta_0$ in $\mathcal D\prime(\mathbb R^n)$; equivalently $-\Delta_x\Phi(x-y)=\delta_y$ for any $y$.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: §2.6.1–2.6.2 flux and distributional interpretation, printed pp.33–34

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
references.locator: §2.1 fundamental solution and flux, printed pp.11–12

items.strategy: Use the earlier local-integrability lemma and Countable Choice embedding to realize Φ as a regular distribution. For a real test, choose R strictly outside its compact support and excise a small ball. The annulus is a bounded C1 domain: the earlier level-2 flux example constructs sphere graph charts and fixes the inner normal. Apply the second Green identity. The inner flux term is the normalized spherical average and tends to φ(0); the Φ∂νφ term vanishes at O(ε) or O(ε|log ε|). Dominated convergence under the local L1 majorant shows the omitted volume integral vanishes. Use the distributional derivative and Dirac definitions; split complex tests and translate the identity via measure-preserving translation.

items.title: Newtonian potential of compactly supported data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported $f$, define $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class. The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself makes no unconditional convergence claim.
items.strategy: Use the explicit locally integrable Borel kernel and, under Countable Choice, replace the measurable source by a Borel representative equal almost everywhere. Tonelli makes the absolute section integral measurable and makes the positive and negative section integrals measurable. The original and Borel representatives give the same integral at each fixed x because they differ only on a null set. On the measurable set where the absolute section integral is finite, their difference defines a measurable Newtonian potential; when that set has full measure, extending across its null complement defines the almost-everywhere class. The point value of the kernel at its pole is immaterial because each singleton is null. Do not assert unconditional finiteness; bounded and L1 convergence are proved by later items.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.title: Distributional derivatives commute with test-function convolution
items.statement: For a distribution T on R^n and a test function φ, every multi-index α satisfies ∂^α(T∗φ)=(∂^αT)∗φ=T∗(∂^αφ), as smooth functions on their common safe domain.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.strategy: Use the published convolution-smoothness theorem and unfold the signed definition of ∂^αT. Differentiate the translation parameter in φ(x−y); integration by parts moves derivatives from the distribution to φ with the two signs cancelling. State the safe domain so no unsupported boundary convolution is implied.

items.title: Bounded compact data give an everywhere finite Newtonian potential
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Suppose the $L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ class $f$ has a finite-valued measurable representative $f_0$ with compact support $K$. Then the Newtonian-potential integral for $f_0$ is absolutely finite at every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, and $Nf_0$ is locally bounded. If $g$ is any finite-valued measurable representative with $g=f_0$ almost everywhere, then its integral is also absolutely finite at every $x$ and equals $Nf_0(x)$ pointwise.

references.title: Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
references.locator: §2.11 Newton-potential definition and absolute convergence, printed p.70

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: §2.6.1 local integrability and §2.7 equation (2.24), printed pp.33,36

items.strategy: Use the essential-supremum bound to reset the representative on a null set and obtain bounded compactly supported data. For each ball of x-values, enclose all x-y with y in the compact support in one centered ball. The affine change of variables y to x-y bounds the kernel integral uniformly by its L1 integral on that ball. Compare any other representative by showing the difference integrand is supported on a measurable null set and hence has zero integral.

items.title: Far-field asymptotics of compact-source Newtonian potentials
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and n≥2. Fix R>0. Let f:R^n→R be Lebesgue measurable, integrable, compactly supported, and zero outside the open Euclidean ball B_R(0); write ||f||_1=∫|f| and M=∫f. For every |x|=r>2R, Nf(x) is absolutely finite. If n≥3, |Nf(x)−M r^(2−n)/((n−2)ω_(n−1))|≤(2^(n−1)R/ω_(n−1))||f||_1 r^(1−n); if n=2, |Nf(x)+M log(r)/(2π)|≤(R/π)||f||_1 r^(−1). The constants are independent of direction. In particular, M=0 gives O(r^(1−n)) for n≥3 and O(r^(−1)) for n=2.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: §2.7, equation (2.24) and exterior asymptotic, printed pp.36–37

references.title: Sung-Jin Oh, Lecture Notes for Math 222A (UC Berkeley, 2024)
references.locator: §4.2, Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.7, printed pp.59–60; application context only

items.strategy: For r=|x|>2R and |y|<R, reverse triangle gives |x−y|>r/2 and ||x−y|−r|≤|y|. Apply the scalar mean value theorem to the explicit radial kernel profile: |Φ(x−y)−Φ(x)|≤(2^(n−1)/ω_(n−1))|y|r^(1−n) for n≥3 and ≤|y|/(πr) for n=2. This proves absolute finiteness and, after writing Φ(x−y)=Φ(x)+(Φ(x−y)−Φ(x)) under the integral, gives the displayed total-mass term and error. The error is uniform in direction and its leading term vanishes when M=0. The proof derives the quantitative remainders locally rather than inferring them from Hunter’s dominated-convergence asymptotic.

items.title: Newtonian potentials solve the distributional Poisson equation
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and n>=2. Let f in L1(R^n) be compactly supported, meaning it has a representative vanishing outside a compact set. Then Nf is finite almost everywhere, belongs to L1_loc(R^n), depends only on the L1 equivalence class, and its regular distribution satisfies -Delta T_Nf=T_f in D′(R^n). This includes C_c data and compactly supported Lp data for every 1<=p<=infinity. If f=0 almost everywhere outside a closed compact set K, then Nf is smooth and harmonic on R^n\K.

references.title: Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
references.locator: §2.11 very weak Poisson identity and Fubini, printed pp.70–71

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.strategy: For a compact test support $K$ and compact support $F$ of $f$, Tonelli gives $\int_K\int_F|\Phi(x-y)f(y)|dy\,dx\le\|f\|_1\sup_{y\in F}\int_K|\Phi(x-y)|dx<\infty$. The local-$L^1$ embedding makes $Nf$ a distribution, and Fubini applies to its pairing. For each $y$, $\int\Phi(x-y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))dx=\varphi(y)$ by the preceding Dirac identity. Exchange the integrals to get $\langle-\Delta Nf,\varphi\rangle=\int f\varphi$. Null representatives agree by Tonelli; finite-measure compact support makes $L^p\subset L^1$ by the published Hölder inequality, including its endpoint. On an open set separated from the compact support, differentiate the smooth kernel under the integral with a uniform distance bound and dominated convergence, then use off-pole harmonicity. Countable Choice is inherited from the kernel and polar proof, not inferred from finite choice.

items.title: Hölder data give a classical Newtonian solution
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge2$, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$0<\alpha<1$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and compactly
supported, with finite global Hölder seminorm
$$[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}:=\sup_{x\ne y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}<\infty.$$
This is the convention for $f\in C_c^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^n)$ here; the
positive-base real power is as in [[def-real-power]]. Put
$\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\mathbb R^n}|f|+[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}$.
Then the Newtonian integral from [[def-newtonian-potential]] is absolutely
finite for every $x$, belongs to $C^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and its second derivatives
are locally $\alpha$-Hölder continuous. In particular
$Nf\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^n)$, where this notation means that
$Nf$ is $C^2$ and each second partial derivative has finite $\alpha$-Hölder
seminorm on every compact set. Moreover,
$$-\Delta Nf(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$
For every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $r>0$ with
$\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_r(x)$, the absolutely convergent cancellation
formula is
$$\partial_i\partial_jNf(x)=\int_{B_r(x)}\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(x-y)\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}f(x),\qquad 0\le i,j<n.$$
For each compact $K\subset\mathbb R^n$, a constant depending only on $n$, $\alpha$
and bounds for $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}f$ satisfies
$$\max_{|\beta|\le2}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\beta Nf(x)|+\max_{|\beta|=2}[\partial^\beta Nf]_{\alpha;K}\le C\,\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}.$$

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: §2.7 Theorem 2.26, Corollary 2.27 and Theorem 2.28, printed pp.37–43

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.strategy: Cut off the pole in $\Phi$ to justify one derivative and bound the removed integrals by $O(\varepsilon)$ (or $O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|)$). For a second derivative subtract $f(x)$ before differentiating $\nabla\Phi$: $|\partial_{ij}\Phi(z)(f(x-z)-f(x))|\le C[f]_\alpha|z|^{\alpha-n}$ is integrable. Apply divergence to the constant part on a ball centered at $x$; the outer spherical flux gives $-\delta_{ij}f(x)/n$, and the cutoff error is $O(\varepsilon^\alpha)$ uniformly on compact $x$ sets. Uniform convergence of the first derivatives and their candidate derivatives proves $C^2$. Compare candidates at $x,x\prime$: split the integrals into $|y-x|\lesssim d=|x-x\prime|$ (bound by $Cd^\alpha$), an outer region (mean-value estimate $|D^3\Phi|\le C|z|^{-n-1}$), and the constant-difference term (annular cancellation of $D^2\Phi$); this gives the stated Hölder seminorm. Apply the published classical/distributional derivative compatibility to this $C^2$ potential and the local-$L^1$ embedding to the continuous difference $-\Delta Nf-f$; the distributional identity then gives pointwise equality. Never differentiate $D^2\Phi*f$ absolutely without subtraction.

items.title: Dirichlet Green function for minus Laplacian
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, a Dirichlet Green function for $-\Delta$ is a function $G_\Omega(x,y)=\Phi(x-y)-H_y(x)$ for $x\ne y$ in $\Omega$, where for each pole $y$, $H_y$ is harmonic on $\Omega$, continuous on $\overline\Omega$, and equals $\Phi(\cdot-y)$ on $\partial\Omega$. Thus $G_\Omega(\cdot,y)$ has zero continuous boundary trace and $-\Delta_xG_\Omega(\cdot,y)=\delta_y$ distributionally. Existence is required, never asserted for every bounded domain.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.title: Puncturing a connected open subset of $\\mathbb{R}^n$ preserves path-connectedness for $n\\ge2$
items.statement: Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, open and connected, and let $y\in\Omega$. Then $\Omega\setminus\{y\}$ is a nonempty, open, connected, path-connected set.

references.title: Paul Bankston, Metric Topology: A First Course, Proposition 21.3
references.locator: Lecture 21, Proposition 21.3, proof that connected open subsets of R^n are path-connected

references.title: N. P. Strickland, Algebraic Topology notes, Proposition 5.14
references.locator: §5, Proposition 5.14, proof that S^n is path-connected for n>0

items.strategy: Start with a finite polygonal path in the open connected set. Choose a small closed ball around the removed point and replace each of the finitely many path intervals inside it by a path on its boundary sphere. Finite pasting gives a path avoiding the point.

items.title: A bounded-domain Dirichlet Green function is unique and positive
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty, open and connected, and suppose a Dirichlet Green function as in [[def-dirichlet-green-function-for-minus-laplacian]] exists. Then it is unique and $G_\Omega(x,y)>0$ for every distinct $x,y\in\Omega$. No boundary differentiability is needed, and existence is not asserted.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
references.locator: §5.4 Theorem 5.21 and Lemma 5.23, uniqueness and positivity, printed pp.124–127

references.title: Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
references.locator: §2.8 Green-function uniqueness and sign remarks, printed pp.44–45

items.strategy: For uniqueness, subtract the two harmonic correctors at each pole and use the weak maximum and minimum principles with their common continuous boundary values. For positivity, derive $\Phi(x-y)\to+\infty$ from its logarithmic or power formula while the corrector stays locally bounded. Weak minimum gives nonnegativity away from a sufficiently small closed ball. The local puncture lemma makes $\Omega\setminus\{y\}$ a connected open set; the strong maximum principle for $-G$ then excludes any zero because $G$ is positive near the pole.

items.title: Symmetry of the Dirichlet Green function
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain carrying a Dirichlet Green function whose harmonic corrector $H_y$ belongs to $C^2(\overline\Omega)$ for every pole $y$. Then $G_\Omega(x,y)=G_\Omega(y,x)$ for all distinct $x,y\in\Omega$. The $C^2$ closure hypothesis licenses the cited classical second Green identity on each twice-punctured domain.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.strategy: Fix distinct poles $x,y$ and prove the identity on $D_\varepsilon=\Omega\setminus(\overline B_\varepsilon(x)\cup\overline B_\varepsilon(y))$. Show this is a nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain even if disconnected, with hole normals $-(z-a)/\varepsilon$. Apply the second Green identity to $u(z)=G_\Omega(z,x)$ and $v(z)=G_\Omega(z,y)$; the volume term vanishes by harmonicity and the outer boundary term by the zero traces. Compute each hole contribution separately from the radial derivative $\Phi_n\prime(\varepsilon)=-1/(\omega_{n-1}\varepsilon^{n-1})$: the sphere about $x$ tends to $G_\Omega(x,y)$ and the sphere about $y$ to $-G_\Omega(y,x)$. Bound the smooth-factor errors by $O(\varepsilon)$ for $n\ge3$ and $O(\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|))$ for $n=2$, then pass to the limit.

items.title: Poisson kernel from a Dirichlet Green function
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and the regularity hypotheses of the Green symmetry theorem. For $x\in\Omega$ and $y\in\partial\Omega$, define $P_\Omega(x,y)=-\partial_{\nu_y}G_\Omega(x,y)$, differentiating in the boundary variable $y$ with the published outward normal. Symmetry identifies this derivative with the first-variable trace of the already regular Green function; no Sobolev or conormal trace is implicit.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.title: Green representation for classical Poisson data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and the Green symmetry/Poisson-kernel regularity hypotheses on a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$. For real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ and $x\in\Omega$, $$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_\Omega(x,y)(-\Delta u(y))dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}P_\Omega(x,y)u(y)dS(y).$$ Both integrals are absolutely finite. Moreover $P_\Omega\ge0$ and $\int_{\partial\Omega}P_\Omega(x,y)dS(y)=1$.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)

items.title: Zero-Dirichlet Green representation for Poisson data
items.statement: Assume the hypotheses and sign convention of the Green representation theorem. If u∈C²(Ω̄), u|∂Ω=0 and f=−Δu, then u(x)=∫_Ω G_Ω(x,y)f(y)dy for every x∈Ω.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern

items.strategy: Specialize the established representation: its boundary term is the Poisson-kernel integral of u|∂Ω and vanishes. Keep the interior sign f=−Δu and the same regularity/integrability hypotheses, rather than asserting an unqualified weak-boundary formula.

items.title: Uniqueness of classical Dirichlet and compatible Neumann solutions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, $n\ge2$. In $C^2(\overline\Omega)$, fixed source $-\Delta u=f$ and fixed Dirichlet trace determine at most one solution; when a Green function with the preceding regularity exists, its representation gives the same conclusion. Fixed source and fixed outward Neumann trace determine solutions up to an additive constant, and solvability requires $\int_\Omega f=-\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_\nu u\,dS$. Existence is not asserted.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.strategy:
Subtract two solutions. For Dirichlet data either use the published bounded-domain uniqueness theorem or subtract the two Green representation formulas: both source and boundary differences vanish. For Neumann data put $w=u-v$ in the published first Green identity, with $\Delta w=0$ and $\partial_
u w=0$; obtain $\int|
abla w|^2=0$. Continuity of the gradient and connectedness imply $w$ is constant. Apply the published divergence theorem to $
abla u$ to get $\int f=-\int\partial_
u u$. Countable Choice is inherited from the integration identities, and no Neumann existence follows from compatibility.

items.title: Necessary compatibility for the classical Neumann Poisson problem
items.statement: Assume Ω is bounded with C¹ boundary, u∈C²(Ω̄), f=−Δu, and outward normal derivative g=∂_νu on ∂Ω. Then ∫_Ω f=−∫_∂Ω g.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.strategy: Apply the published divergence theorem to ∇u: ∫_Ω Δu=∫_∂Ω ∂_νu. Substitute f=−Δu. State the outward-normal convention and apply real/imaginary parts separately for complex u.

items.title: Classical Neumann solutions differ by componentwise constants
items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when $n\ge2$. Assume $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is a bounded $C^1$ domain with finitely many connected components. If $u,v\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ solve the same Poisson equation and have the same outward normal derivative on $\partial\Omega$, then $u-v$ is constant on each connected component. In particular it is constant when $\Omega$ is connected.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.strategy: Set w=u−v. Then Δw=0 and ∂_νw=0. Apply the first Green identity to w on each component (to real and imaginary parts if needed): ∫|∇w|²=0. Continuity of ∇w gives ∇w=0, and connectedness yields a constant on each component. Do not assert one common constant on a disconnected domain.

items.title: The Green identities used here are Euclidean
items.statement: Every boundary flux on this page uses the earlier Euclidean surface-measure, divergence and Green identities, with outward normals reversed on excised balls. The later manifold Stokes theorem is orientation context only and supplies no proof step here. All such uses inherit the earlier Countable Choice premise.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

title: Fundamental Solutions Newtonian Potentials and Green Functions — Examples

items.title: Flux normalization on every centered sphere
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For every $r>0$, with the outward normal of $B_r(0)$, $-\int_{\partial B_r}\partial_\nu\Phi\,dS=1$; the same calculation works for the logarithmic $n=2$ kernel.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026 complete lecture notes)
references.locator: §2.1 definition and flux-normalization remark, printed pp. 12–13; flux assertion is assigned as an exercise-class verification and Schmidt's kernel is the negative of this pair's kernel

items.strategy: Differentiate both radial formulas to obtain $\partial_r\Phi=-1/(\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1})$, including $\omega_1=2\pi$. Multiply by $|\partial B_r|=\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}$ in the published chart/polar surface convention. Distinguish this ball-outward normal from the opposite normal on an excised inner boundary.

items.title: The two-dimensional logarithmic kernel has unit normalized flux
items.statement: For Φ(x)=−(2π)^(−1)log|x| on R²∖{0}, the outward flux through every circle ∂B_r is ∫_∂B_r ∂_νΦ ds=−1, equivalently −∫_∂B_r ∂_νΦ ds=1 for the positive operator −Δ.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.strategy: Differentiate radially to obtain ∂_rΦ=−1/(2πr), multiply by circumference 2πr, and check the inward normal on an excised inner boundary reverses this sign. This is the n=2 normalization behind −ΔΦ=δ_0.

items.title: Adding an entire harmonic function preserves a Laplace fundamental solution
items.statement: If −ΔE=δ_0 in distributions on R^n and h is an entire classical harmonic function, then −Δ(E+h)=δ_0. Thus the fundamental solution is not unique without an extra growth or normalization condition.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.strategy: Embed the smooth h as a regular distribution, use linearity of distributional differentiation, and use Δh=0 pointwise. Then −Δ(E+h)=−ΔE−Δh=δ_0. A nonzero constant already gives a distinct kernel.

items.title: Newtonian potential of radial compact data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, $n\ge2$, and $f(x)=\rho(|x|)\in C_c^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^n)$, $0<\alpha<1$. Then $u=Nf$ is radial, $u\prime(r)=-r^{1-n}\int_0^r s^{n-1}\rho(s)ds$ for $r>0$, and $u(r)=u(0)-\int_0^r t^{1-n}\int_0^t s^{n-1}\rho(s)ds\,dt$. Here $u(0)=(n-2)^{-1}\int_0^\infty s\rho(s)ds$ for $n\ge3$, while $u(0)=-\int_0^\infty s\log s\,\rho(s)ds$ for $n=2$.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
Thomas Schmidt, Partial Differential Equations I (2026)
references.locator: §2.11 Newton potential and radial ODE, printed pp.69–72

items.strategy: Rotational invariance of the kernel and Lebesgue measure makes $u$ radial. The classical theorem supplies $C^2$ and $-\Delta u=\rho(r)$. Multiply the radial equation by $r^{n-1}$ and integrate from $0$, using regularity to get $r^{n-1}u\prime(r)\to0$. Integrate again to obtain the displayed one-dimensional formula. Evaluate $u(0)$ directly from the defining integral by polar coordinates, treating $n=2$ logarithmic integrability separately. The formula tests both the sign and normalization without invoking the later shell example.

items.title: Newton shell theorem from harmonic mean values
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, $n\ge3$, $R>0$, and a shell of total mass $M$ uniformly distributed on $\partial B_R(0)$. Its potential $U(x)=M|\partial B_R|^{-1}\int_{\partial B_R}\Phi(x-y)dS_y$ equals $M\Phi(x)$ for $|x|>R$ and equals $M\Phi(R)$ for $|x|<R$.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)

items.strategy: For $|x|>R$, the function $y\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B_R$, so the published spherical mean theorem gives its average as $\Phi(x)$. For $|x|<R$, the shell integral is a continuous radial harmonic function of $x$ because the pole stays outside each compact subball and kernel derivatives are uniformly bounded there. The radial harmonic ODE yields $a+b|x|^{2-n}$; regularity at zero forces $b=0$. Evaluate at zero to get $M\Phi(R)$. The surface measure and mean-value premises require Countable Choice.

items.title: The fundamental Hessian is not absolutely locally integrable
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Every nonzero Cartesian second derivative $\partial_{ij}\Phi$ has $|\partial_{ij}\Phi|\notin L^1(B_\varepsilon(0))$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, although the signed kernel has annular cancellation. Thus the formal absolutely convergent integral $\int\partial_{ij}\Phi(x-y)f(y)dy$ can fail at a point with $f(x)\ne0$.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript)

items.strategy: Use $\partial_{ij}\Phi(r\omega)=c_n r^{-n}(n\omega_i\omega_j-\delta_{ij})$. For either diagonal or off-diagonal indices the angular factor is nonzero on a spherical open set of positive surface measure. Polar integration of its absolute value gives a positive constant times $\int_0^\varepsilon dr/r=\infty$. The signed angular integral is zero by symmetry, explaining why the prior Hölder-data theorem subtracts $f(x)$ and includes a boundary correction.

items.title: An isolated boundary point obstructs pointwise-zero Green data
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For $\Omega=B_1(0)\setminus\{0\}$, no Dirichlet Green function exists in the preceding naive pointwise-zero-boundary sense: for a pole $y\in\Omega$, a harmonic corrector continuous on $\overline\Omega$ cannot equal $\Phi(\cdot-y)$ both on $\partial B_1$ and at the isolated boundary point $0$. This does not deny weaker potential-theoretic Green kernels.

items.strategy: For fixed $y\ne0$, use the published smooth-sphere-data replacement on $B_1$ for boundary data $\Phi(\cdot-y)$, obtaining $H_B$. Then $G_B=\Phi(\cdot-y)-H_B$ satisfies the local Green definition on the ball, so positivity gives $G_B(0,y)>0$. If a punctured-ball corrector $H_\Omega$ existed, its difference from $H_B$ would be harmonic on $B_1\setminus\{0\}$, bounded near zero by the claimed continuous trace, and zero on the outer sphere. The published removable-singularity theorem extends the difference harmonically across zero; the weak maximum/minimum principle forces it to vanish. But the two prescribed values at zero differ by $G_B(0,y)>0$, contradiction. This uses only an example-side ball construction; the general spine asserts no Green existence.

items.title: Neumann Poisson data require a flux compatibility equation
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $\Omega$ be a bounded nonempty $C^1$ domain, $n\ge2$. A $C^2(\overline\Omega)$ solution of $-\Delta u=f$, $\partial_\nu u=g$ must satisfy $\int_\Omega f=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS$. In particular $f\equiv1$, $g\equiv0$ has no such solution, even though each datum is smooth.

items.strategy: Apply the published divergence theorem to $\nabla u$; the chosen minus-Laplacian convention gives the negative sign. For the explicit data, the left integral is $|\Omega|>0$ while the right side is zero, so no classical solution exists. The example does not claim compatibility suffices for existence.

items.title: One-dimensional Dirichlet Green kernel on an interval
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For $a<b$ and $x,y\in(a,b)$, the one-dimensional Dirichlet kernel for $-d^2/dx^2$ is $G(x,y)=((\min\{x,y\}-a)(b-\max\{x,y\}))/(b-a)$. It is symmetric, nonnegative, vanishes at $a,b$, and its $x$-derivative has jump $\partial_xG(y+,y)-\partial_xG(y-,y)=-1$, so $-\partial_x^2G(\cdot,y)=\delta_y$ in $\mathcal D'(a,b)$. Its difference from $-|x-y|/2$ is affine in $x$. The stated Countable Choice assumption is used for the named Lebesgue-measure and regular-distribution interfaces below; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

items.strategy: Write the two affine formulas for $x<y$ and $x>y$. Their values agree at $x=y$ and equal zero at the appropriate endpoints. Direct differentiation gives slopes $(b-y)/(b-a)$ and $-(y-a)/(b-a)$, whose right-minus-left jump is $-1$. Integrating by parts separately on $(a,y)$ and $(y,b)$ against a compact test function proves the Dirac identity. Swapping $x,y$ leaves the min/max formula unchanged; subtracting the one-dimensional fundamental kernel cancels the slope jump and leaves a globally affine harmonic corrector.
